The rating is Medium: realized automatability of broad survey content is genuine but not yet dominant given low near-term instructional diffusion.

By 2031, AI will competently synthesize and explain the full span of introductory business-of-sport content this course covers, from marketing and finance basics to legal and governance overviews, and will do so with limited need for expert correction on foundational material. The course's gateway role for later required sport-management courses offers only mild protection at this horizon since the F5 cap here binds solely at 24 months. Career-advising content retains a human, relational residue, but it is a modest share of the syllabus. The rating rises to High: the instrumental case for a student needing this specific course to acquire introductory sport-business knowledge is substantially eroded by broadly capable, low-verification-burden AI explanation and synthesis.

A decade out, AI systems plausibly deliver personalized, adaptive introductions to sport-industry marketing, finance, facilities, and governance more efficiently than a fixed-syllabus survey course, and diffusion into higher-education content delivery is likely to be far more advanced than today's roughly one-in-five firm adoption rate suggests for 2036. The rating holds High, reflecting that the applied knowledge-transmission function of this specific course is largely substitutable. The hedge is real: capability-versus-adoption gaps in higher-education curricula specifically are historically slow to close, accreditation and advising norms could preserve a human-taught gateway course regardless of content automatability, and career-development advising may retain durable value that a survey syllabus does not capture. Confidence in the direction is higher than confidence in the pace, and the ten-year point estimate should be read as a central tendency, not a certainty.

A variety of topics will be explored including marketing, facilities, operations, finance, legal and ethical issues, media and governance. The content focuses on sport management and business functions required within the sport industry while introducing professional development and career options.

r: SM 2300 is explicitly practicum-style: students join committees to plan, organize, publicize, and manage a real sport event, and all students must commit to attending and working the culminating event itself. By 2031, AI will more capably draft event-marketing materials, staffing schedules, and sponsor communications, further automating the administrative planning layer of event management. But the course's central requirement — physically staffing and executing a live event, resolving unpredictable real-time problems, and coordinating people and vendors in person — remains an embodied, presence-dependent task that generative and reasoning models do not perform. The dampening effect of that embodied core persists across the horizon: verification of on-site event execution requires a human physically present, not a model output. Diffusion of AI into event-day operations specifically is not plausible on this timescale given the physical and coordination demands involved. The rating rises modestly to Medium, reflecting that the planning-and-publicity share of coursework is increasingly AI-assisted even as the event-day embodied requirement continues to anchor the course's instrumental necessity.

A decade out, AI-assisted event-planning software, automated scheduling, and generative publicity content will plausibly handle much of the administrative planning this course teaches, and capability growth in agentic task execution is fast by the METR/Epoch trend. Even so, the requirement that students personally staff and operate a live event — the course's explicit, non-negotiable culminating requirement — keeps a substantial embodied, real-time-coordination core that resists substitution; task-exposure frameworks consistently place hands-on public-facing event operations among the least automatable activity categories. The rating holds Medium, hedged because the balance between planning automation and hands-on execution could shift further toward automation if venue technology and event robotics mature faster than a central-case forecast assumes, and because ten-year predictions about event-operations practice carry real uncertainty in either direction.

The rating rises to High, reflecting that the applied research and analytical-writing tasks the course centers on become largely automatable given a decade of compounding capability gains, though this is meaningfully hedged: task-exposure research's negative association between critical-thinking skill and exposure may hold up longer than a pure capability trend suggests, and ten-year forecasts carry substantial uncertainty about whether ethical-judgment tasks like these remain a genuine human residue.
SM 3700.d: Students examine sustainability within the sport industry, focusing on management, products, and experiences. They analyze strategies to enhance positive and reduce negative cultural, environmental, and economic impacts. Through global case studies, students explore ethical decision-making, environmental stewardship, and sustainable management practices in sport organizations.

r: Sport Analytics introduces students to analytical techniques applied across team management, athlete performance, human resources, marketing, finance, and facility and event management, with an emphasis on running the analyses and understanding career paths in the field. Task-exposure research explicitly names quantitative analysts and mathematicians among the most-exposed occupations, and this course's core activity, applying analytical techniques to structured sport-business data, maps directly onto that category. Observed-usage data shows Computer & Mathematical work as the largest current AI-usage category, and generative and analytical tools already run regressions, build dashboards, and interpret results competently across the domains this course surveys. Verification burden is moderate: analytic outputs feeding real personnel, marketing, or facility decisions still warrant a knowledgeable human check. The rating is High already at 24 months because the applied technique the course teaches is precisely the kind of quantitative work current AI systems already perform well.

By 2031, AI will plausibly execute the great majority of the analytical workflow this course surveys, data preparation, statistical modeling, and dashboard generation across athlete performance, marketing, finance, and facility domains, with far broader diffusion into sport organizations than exists today. Task-exposure research's strongest exposure signal applies directly to quantitative analysis work, and no licensure, embodiment, or foundational-scaffolding constraint caps the course, since it functions as an elective survey rather than a gateway to later required coursework. The rating is High: the applied technique itself becomes producible with limited human input, leaving human analysts concentrated on framing questions and interpreting results for organizational decisions, a real but narrower residue than the course's full technical content, which is why the instrumental need to learn the mechanics directly is substantially eroded.

A decade out, AI plausibly runs sport-analytics workflows end to end, from data ingestion through modeling to decision-ready output, across the team-management, marketing, and facility domains this course surveys, consistent with capability-growth trends showing AI task-handling horizons compounding rapidly. The rating holds High, extending the prior horizons, since no institutional constraint offers a floor. The hedge is real: ten-year capability projections carry wide uncertainty, and it is plausible that framing analytical questions and validating outputs against organizational context sustains meaningful human analyst roles even as execution automates. Still, the specific instrumental skill this course conveys, running analytical techniques on sport-business data, sits inside the task category evidence most consistently identifies as highly exposed, leaving little basis to expect the course's mechanics-focused content to retain its current necessity.
SM 4350.d: The main objective of this course is to introduce students to the emerging field of analytics in the sport industry. The course will discuss the impact and challenges of analytics on team management, athlete performance, human resources, marketing, finance, law, manufacturing, event management, and facility management. Students will also learn how these analytical techniques are run and explore career options in sport analytics.

r: Organization and Administration of Sports examines how sport agencies are structured and managed, covering managerial functions, leadership, organizational effectiveness, and human-resource management within sport organizations. Much of this analytical and administrative knowledge work, drafting policy, structuring HR processes, evaluating organizational effectiveness, is exposed to AI, and observed-usage data shows management-related tasks rising as a share of current AI use. But management in a sport-organization context retains a real interpersonal core: leading staff, coaches, and stakeholders, and handling the personnel judgment calls administration requires. With no institutional lock on this general-administration course and only moderate verification burden, the rating is Medium at 24 months: AI competently supports managerial analysis and HR documentation, partially eroding the instrumental case, while the interpersonal leadership content and limited current diffusion into sport-organization HR workflows keep the erosion incomplete.

By 2031, AI will plausibly handle much of the analytical and administrative work of sport-organization management, HR policy drafting, organizational-effectiveness reporting, structural analysis, with diffusion into athletic administration considerably broader than today. No licensure or foundational-scaffolding constraint protects the course; it stands adjacent to, not prerequisite for, other required Sport Management coursework. The interpersonal residue, leading and motivating staff, resolving personnel conflict, is real but is a modest fraction of the course's total content, which spans HR, organizational structure, and administrative theory broadly. The rating rises to High: the applied administrative-knowledge work is performed competently by AI with limited human drafting input for most tasks, leaving human administrators concentrated on the interpersonal leadership dimension that the course covers alongside its more automatable managerial-analysis content.

A decade out, AI is plausibly deeply embedded in sport-organization administrative workflows, handling HR documentation, policy analysis, and organizational-effectiveness evaluation, with human administrators concentrated on interpersonal leadership and contested personnel decisions. The rating holds High, extending the five-year trajectory, since no accreditation floor or clinical-hours requirement offers protection at this horizon. The hedge is genuine: sport organizations are relationship-driven institutions, and it remains possible that leadership and stakeholder-management skills sustain more direct human administrative work than a pure capability read implies, while ten-year capability and diffusion trajectories carry real uncertainty. Still, the bulk of what this survey course teaches, administrative and managerial mechanics rather than the interpersonal leadership residue alone, sits in task categories that evidence consistently associates with high automation exposure.
SM 4600.d: This upper division course focuses on the organization, administration, and management of agencies within the sport industry. Students will examine and evaluate the varying attributes of sport organizations and common managerial functions. Emphasis will be placed on leadership, organizational effectiveness, and human resource management.

r: The Sport Enterprise surveys economics, budgeting, and finance as applied to the sport industry, covering venue and franchise financing, event and collegiate-athletics finance, and related legal considerations. Financial analysis, budgeting, and legal-research support are among the knowledge-work tasks most exposed to AI, and observed-usage data shows Computer & Mathematical and writing-adjacent tasks prominent in current AI use, with tools already competently drafting budget models and summarizing financing structures. Verification burden is real, however, financing and legal analysis errors carry organizational cost, so outputs still warrant a knowledgeable check, and diffusion of these tools into sport-specific finance work remains uneven this early. With no institutional lock on this survey course, the rating is Medium at 24 months: AI meaningfully assists the financial and legal analysis the course covers without yet fully substituting for the student's own applied learning.

By 2031, AI will plausibly perform the bulk of the financial modeling, budgeting, and legal-research support this course teaches, franchise valuation, venue financing structures, event budgeting, with far more complete diffusion into sport-business analysis than exists today. No licensure, embodiment, or foundational-scaffolding constraint caps the course, which functions as an elective survey of sport-business finance rather than a gateway to required coursework. The rating rises to High: the applied financial and legal analysis is producible competently with limited human input for most routine tasks, though verification burden around high-stakes financing and legal decisions keeps a residual human-check role in place. The instrumental case for learning these mechanics directly is substantially eroded at this horizon, even as the residual oversight role retains some value.

A decade out, AI plausibly handles most routine financial and legal analysis in sport-business finance, budget modeling, financing-structure evaluation, contract-adjacent legal summarization, consistent with rapid capability-growth trends, with human involvement concentrated on high-stakes negotiation and verification of consequential financing and legal decisions. The rating holds High, extending the five-year trajectory, since no accreditation floor protects this survey course. The hedge is genuine: financing and legal work carries real error cost, and it remains plausible that verification-heavy oversight roles sustain more direct human involvement in sport-enterprise finance than a pure capability projection implies, while ten-year forecasts carry substantial uncertainty. Still, the applied budgeting and financial-analysis mechanics this course centers on sit within task categories that evidence consistently identifies as highly exposed to AI performance.
SM 4610.d: This survey course explores principles of economics, budgeting, and finance as applied to the sport industry. Specific topics include sport venues and franchise financing along with events, professional sport, collegiate athletics, and industry finance, budgeting, and legal considerations.

r: This capstone seminar has students synthesize concepts and analytical tools from across the Sport Management curriculum, applying theory to strategic-planning case studies and producing a formal White Paper analyzing a specific area of the sport industry. Professional-writing tasks are strongly exposed to AI, productivity research finds substantial time savings and quality gains on writing tasks of this kind, and AI already drafts research summaries and structures analytical papers competently. But the course's core requirement is cross-course synthesis and strategic judgment applied to real case scenarios, work that leans toward the critical-thinking category task-exposure research finds more resistant to exposure. With no institutional lock on this culminating elective course, the rating is Medium at 24 months: AI meaningfully assists the White Paper's drafting and research components while the integrative strategic-analysis work the seminar is built around remains substantially the student's own.

By 2031, AI will plausibly draft the majority of the White Paper's research synthesis and structural writing, and will competently model strategic-planning scenarios similar to the seminar's case studies, with far broader diffusion of these tools into student and professional research workflows than today, consistent with the general diffusion trend of AI adoption climbing well beyond current levels. No licensure or foundational-scaffolding constraint caps the rating, and the course sits at the end of the curriculum rather than as a prerequisite for later required work. The rating rises to High: the applied deliverable, a synthesized, well-argued White Paper drawing on strategic concepts, becomes producible competently with limited human drafting input, even though the specific critical-thinking and ethical-decision-making skills the seminar aims to develop retain some protective value against full exposure at this horizon.

A decade out, AI plausibly performs most of the analytical synthesis and writing this capstone requires, integrating concepts across a curriculum, structuring strategic arguments, producing polished analytical documents, consistent with capability-growth trends compounding over a decade. The rating holds High, extending the five-year trajectory, since no accreditation floor or clinical-hours requirement protects this elective seminar. The hedge is genuine: task-exposure research's finding that critical-thinking skills resist exposure more than routine writing may sustain more human involvement in the seminar's ethical-decision-making and strategic-judgment components than a pure capability read implies, and ten-year forecasts carry real uncertainty. Still, the deliverable-producing mechanics this capstone centers on, research synthesis and structured writing, sit within the task category evidence consistently identifies as among the most exposed.
SM 4860.d: This capstone course for Sport Management students will draw upon and connect the concepts and analytical tools students have developed in all previous Sport Management courses. Students will be required to synthesize and apply theories, concepts, and practices when engaging in specific strategic planning situations and case studies. Emphasis will be placed on critical thinking and ethical decision-making skills. A formal White Paper, which will provide opportunities for in-depth analysis and explanation of a specific area within the sport industry, is also required. This paper is intended to provide students further insight into the sport industry and to offer additional practical application of knowledge and experience.

r: The Sport Management internship places students in a 405-hour applied placement with a sport organization or agency, under joint faculty and site-supervisor oversight, to apply program knowledge and skills in a real, non-classroom workplace. The defining feature is embodied, real-time presence: representing the host organization, executing event-day operations, coordinating with staff and the public, and performing the physical and interpersonal work of a sport-industry job, task-exposure research places real-time, in-person coordination and physical-presence work squarely in its low-exposure categories. Some administrative sub-tasks within the placement, reporting, scheduling support, correspondence drafting, are individually AI-exposed, but the course's instrumental requirement is the supervised, embodied placement itself, not any single deliverable. The rating is Low at 24 months: the requirement to physically occupy and perform the internship role is untouched by current AI capability.

By 2031, AI will plausibly handle more of the administrative sub-tasks within a typical sport-industry placement, scheduling, reporting, correspondence, some analytics, but the internship's defining requirement remains a student's embodied presence at a host site, executing real-time operational and interpersonal work under supervision. Verification burden matters here too: site supervisors and faculty evaluate performance in situ, a form of oversight AI cannot substitute for. No accreditation-mandated clinical-hours floor is documented for this program, so the protection here rests on embodiment rather than a hard institutional lock, a comparatively softer constraint than clinical licensure fields carry. The rating rises to Medium: as the office-adjacent components of sport-organization work become more AI-assisted, the placement's non-administrative core still requires the student's physical, real-time participation, though the erosion of surrounding tasks is real.

A decade out, AI-assisted tools will plausibly be standard within host sport organizations for reporting, scheduling, and analytics support, further eroding the administrative slice of what an intern does day to day. But the requirement that a student physically occupy a role, coordinate with people in real time, and be evaluated on hands-on performance persists as the internship's defining feature, and no plausible capability trajectory eliminates the value of that embodied, supervised experience. The rating holds Medium, reflecting that automatable administrative sub-tasks continue shrinking while the placement's embodied core remains necessary. The hedge is genuine: remote and hybrid internship models could expand over ten years in ways that reduce presence requirements, a real, if currently undocumented, source of uncertainty for the course's future structure.
SM 4890.d: The Sport Management internship is a culminating 9 credit/405 hour applied experience with a sport organization or agency. The course is planned with, and supervised by, faculty and site supervisors. The goal of the internship is to provide the student with the opportunity to utilize knowledge and skills developed throughout the Sport Management curriculum in a non-classroom setting.

r: This course paired with the internship has students build professional dispositions, business etiquette, and career-development skills, producing a detailed internship and career-goals report and a professional portfolio. Portfolio and report writing are exposed tasks, task-exposure research finds writing strongly positively associated with AI exposure, and generative tools already draft resume content, career narratives, and reflective reports competently. But a meaningful share of the course is live professional-development practice, etiquette coaching, interpersonal disposition-building, discussion of on-the-job internship experiences, which retains an interpersonal, real-time component AI does not replace. With no institutional lock and moderate verification burden around the quality of self-presentation materials, the rating is Medium at 24 months: AI meaningfully assists the written deliverables while the interpersonal coaching and disposition-development activities the course is built around remain substantially in-person and instructor-led.

By 2031, AI will plausibly draft the bulk of the portfolio and career-goals report content this course requires, and will competently model interview and networking practice scenarios, with far broader diffusion of career-coaching AI tools than exists today. No licensure or foundational-scaffolding constraint caps the course, and it functions as a companion to the internship rather than a prerequisite for further required coursework. The rating rises to High: the written deliverables and much of the self-presentation coaching content become producible or practicable with AI assistance, and observed-usage data already shows writing and office tasks as a leading current AI-use category. The interpersonal etiquette and disposition components retain some protective value, but they are a narrower slice of the course's graded content than the portfolio and reporting requirements.

A decade out, AI-assisted career coaching, portfolio drafting, and interview practice will plausibly be commonplace, consistent with capability-growth trends compounding over a decade, and much of what this course formally teaches, how to build a professional portfolio and articulate career goals, becomes something AI can competently support directly. The rating holds High, extending the five-year trajectory, since no accreditation floor protects this companion course. The hedge is genuine: in-person professional disposition and etiquette coaching may retain more instructional value than a pure capability read suggests, since interpersonal presentation is itself part of what employers evaluate, and ten-year forecasts carry real uncertainty about how career-services instruction evolves. Still, the writing-heavy deliverables this course centers on sit within the most consistently exposed task category in the evidence base.
SM 4891.d: This course is designed to provide Sport Management students multiple and varying opportunities to assess and improve their professional dispositions, business etiquette, and career development. In addition, academic assignments related to SM 4890 will be discussed and developed. A detailed internship and career goals report and professional portfolio related to the internship experiences are required. Surveying
